Cower

/COW-er/ — rhymes with tower · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To cower is to crouch down or shrink back in fear, making yourself smaller to avoid a threat.

The puppy cowered behind the sofa during the thunderstorm.

Worked Example

When the bully approached with an angry expression, the smaller student cowered against the lockers, hunching down and turning away to appear smaller.

Cower precisely names the physical act of crouching down and shrinking back in fear, which is far more vivid and specific than simply saying 'was afraid.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tremble: To tremble is to shake with small, continuous movements from fear or cold — the fear shows, but the body stays where it is. To cower goes further: the whole body crouches and shrinks away, trying to look smaller until the threat passes.

cringe: To cringe is to shrink back with a quick, tightening jerk of the face and shoulders, from fear or even embarrassment. To cower is bigger and longer: the entire body drops low and stays hunched, driven by real fear of a threat.

recoil: To recoil is to spring back suddenly from something frightening or disgusting — one sharp backward motion, and it is over. To cower is sustained: instead of one jump away, the frightened person sinks down and stays crouched, making themselves small before the threat.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

confront: face a threat directly and bravely

defy: boldly refuse to obey or back down

Where it sits · how much fear takes over the body — flinch → crouch → shrink → cower

flinch vs. cower: Flinch is weaker than cower: a flinch is a split-second jerk of fear, while cowering means your whole body stays crouched and shrinking from the threat.

crouch vs. cower: Crouch is weaker than cower because it carries no fear at all — a baseball catcher crouches by choice, but a person who cowers is bent low because terror has taken over.

shrink vs. cower: Shrink comes close to cower, but cower is stronger — shrinking is pulling back from something unpleasant, while cowering is collapsing into a trembling huddle of pure fear.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cower

Root — cower: to squat, huddle, or lie low (Middle English (from Middle Low German or Scandinavian))

Put it together

Put it together: Cower is a single root that entered English from a northern European word for squatting or hunkering down — the crouching, shrinking-back posture is built into the word's entire history, and fear was added to its meaning over time.

Use the root in a new word: cowering

Use the root in a new word: cowering: The cowering kitten pressed itself flat under the porch during the fireworks — exactly what you would expect from an animal that cowers at every loud noise.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral / literary

Cower is the vivid word for someone physically retreating in fear—crouching down and shrinking. Use it when you need to show fear as an action, not just an emotion. 'Hide' or 'crouch' alone are simpler; 'cower' adds the layer of fear driving the movement.
